articles.title: Delhi's massive vehicle ban faces its biggest test at the borders: Can enforcement keep up?
articles.summary: Delhi’s decision to stop older vehicles not meeting BS6 norms from entering the capital brings the focus back to a challenge that is more than announcing
articles.body: Delhi’s decision to stop older vehicles not meeting BS6 norms from entering the capital brings the focus back to a challenge that is more than announcing restrictions, that of implementing them. With potentially more than 10 lakh vehicles from neighboring NCR cities affected, the success of the move will depend less on the rule itself, and more on how effectively authorities are able to identify, intercept and turn away vehicles at Delhi's numerous entry points.The exercise is on scale. Vehicles from Gurgaon, Faridabad, Noida, Greater Noida and Ghaziabad enter Delhi through a number of busy roads, many of which witness heavy traffic during morning and evening peak hours. It’s neither practical nor sustainable to check each vehicle manually. Even if teams from the traffic police and the transport department are deployed at major entry points, the volume of traffic could quickly overwhelm available manpower.The tech testTechnology will be important in enforcement, therefore. Cameras using automatic number plate recognition, linked to vehicle registration databases, can help to identify vehicles that do not meet prescribed emission standards. But the system will only work if the cameras cover key entry points, registration records are up to date and enforcement teams can act on the alerts as they happen.Practical complications also exist. Damaged, obscured or hard to read number plates can affect camera-based identification. Records of vehicles registered outside of Delhi may be incomplete or outdated. Authorities need to have a reliable way of checking these vehicles without increasing the level of congestion at the checkpoints.The gaps along the borderAnother challenge is the sheer number of ways in you can watch the major highways and arterial roads, but smaller roads and connecting stretches may be opportunities to get around the checkpoints. If the enforcement is focused on some high-profile spots, motorists could just find alternative routes into the city. It would also put traffic into residential areas and smaller roads, creating new congestion problems.Delhi and neighboring NCR authorities will have to coordinate equally. Data on vehicle registrations, emission certificates and enforcement should be accessible across the states. Without smooth coordination, vehicles turned away at one checkpoint might try to enter via another route. The exercise would be more effective if there is a common enforcement mechanism across the NCR.Commuters need to knowThe restrictions also have the potential to confuse daily commuters, especially those who travel to Delhi for work, education and business. Authorities will need to clearly communicate which vehicles are allowed, what documents drivers need to carry and how exemptions, if any, will be handled. It is equally important to ensure that enforcement is not arbitrary and that motorists do not face unnecessary delays or disputes at the checkpoints.Beyond the first crackdownThe larger question is whether enforcement can be maintained for the three-month restriction period, from Nov. 1 to Jan. 31. There will be a lot of activity at the initial deployment and checks but the real test will be to see if the monitoring continues at the same intensity after the first few weeks.Authorities should also regularly publish data on the number of vehicles checked, turned away and penalized and details of enforcement at different entry points. Such disclosures would help to ascertain whether the restrictions are being uniformly applied, or whether there are any gaps.In the end, Delhi’s vehicle ban is only as good as its enforcement network. A rule that appears strict on paper will be of little use if thousands of vehicles continue to pass through the borders. The administration will need more than checkpoints and occasional drives, already stressed by winter pollution. articles.title: Be a sport, give your eyes and back a rest: Prolonged gaming, binge-watching raise blood clot risks
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: From gaming marathons to back-to-back OTT episodes, hours spent glued to a screen may be doing more than straining the eyes and back.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: From gaming marathons to back-to-back OTT episodes, hours spent glued to a screen may be doing more than straining the eyes and back. Vascular experts warn that prolonged, uninterrupted sitting can slow blood flow in the legs and increase the risk of potentially dangerous blood clots, including deep vein thrombosis (DVT), even among younger people.At a conference being held in the city from Oct 8 to 10, experts said the concern was not gaming or OTT viewing itself, but the prolonged immobility that can accompany them.Dr Tapish Sahu, organising secretary of VSI-ASVS 2026 and head of vascular and endovascular surgery at Max Hospital, said doctors were seeing young patients with prolonged sitting and excessive screen exposure. "Sitting continuously for four to six hours while gaming or binge-watching leaves the calf muscles largely inactive. Movement breaks must become part of digital life," he said.A 2024 meta-analysis in Scientific Reports, analysing 31 studies, found that people with the highest sedentary behaviour had a 24% higher risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) than those with the lowest levels. Risk rose by about 2% for every additional hour of daily sedentary behaviour.Dr Tarun Grover, senior director of peripheral vascular and endovascular sciences at Medanta, said immobility had traditionally been discussed in the context of long-distance travel, hospitalisation or being bedridden. "Today, we also need to ask young patients how many hours they spend continuously sitting in front of a gaming console, computer or OTT screen," he added.Experts cautioned that screen use does not automatically cause DVT, but prolonged sitting may add to the risk when combined with obesity, dehydration, smoking, hormonal factors, inherited clotting disorders or a previous history of thrombosis.A study published this year involving 11 adolescents with thrombosis found that they used digital devices for an average of six hours daily, with uninterrupted immobility averaging 2.7 hours. Eight had lower-limb DVT, two pulmonary embolism and one subclavian-vein thrombosis. Many also had inherited thrombophilia, suggesting that prolonged screen-related immobility may be an additional risk factor rather than the sole cause.Walking activates the calf muscles, which help pump blood towards the heart.Dr Bhupesh Garg, senior vascular and endovascular surgeon at the Vascular Society of India, said that "smoking adversely affects vascular health and increases thrombosis risk, while prolonged sitting slows blood flow from the legs due to calf muscle inactivity".The experts also stressed that regular exercise may not fully offset the risks of prolonged sitting. For young people, hours in classrooms followed by gaming, streaming or social media can add to their daily sedentary time.DVT occurs when a clot forms in a deep vein, usually in the leg. If it travels to the lungs, it can cause a potentially fatal pulmonary embolism. Swelling, pain or tenderness in one leg warrants medical evaluation, while sudden breathlessness, chest pain or coughing up blood requires urgent medical attention.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: A Georgia high-school student formed a volunteer team to turn backyards, schools and public spaces into wildlife habitat; two years later, Johns Creek became America’s 60th Certified Community Wildlife Habitat
articles.summary: A suburban Georgia community became a model for urban wildlife conservation after teenager Malcolm Barnard led a two-year campaign to turn backyards,
articles.body: A suburban Georgia community became a model for urban wildlife conservation after teenager Malcolm Barnard led a two-year campaign to turn backyards, school grounds and public spaces into wildlife habitats. According to the National Wildlife Federation (NWF), Johns Creek earned its Community Wildlife Habitat certification in 2012, becoming the organisation’s 60th certified community in the United States and only the second in Georgia at the time.Johns Creek, a growing city northeast of Atlanta, might not immediately seem like the setting for a major wildlife initiative. However, Barnard recognised the importance of protecting natural habitats in a rapidly developing suburban environment. According to National Wildlife magazine, he first discovered the NWF’s Community Wildlife Habitat programme while working on a school project. The programme encourages residents to make their properties more welcoming to wildlife by providing essential resources such as food, water, shelter and places where animals can raise their young. Inspired by the initiative, Barnard approached Johns Creek officials with the idea of pursuing certification for the entire city.The effort quickly grew beyond a student project. Barnard assembled a volunteer team and began working with residents, schools, businesses and community organisations. His approach included educating homeowners about wildlife-friendly gardening, encouraging individual properties to seek certification and organising workshops to build support for the initiative. Action for Nature, which later honoured Barnard with its 2013 International Young Eco-Hero award, said he also went door to door to explain why preserving habitat mattered in a rapidly developing community.The campaign also placed schools at the centre of the effort. Barnard secured funding that could be directed towards school habitat gardens, while participating schools received wildlife-habitat signage. By 2013, all 18 of Johns Creek’s public schools had become certified through the NWF’s Schoolyard Habitats programme, according to Action for Nature and other conservation records. The project required a significant amount of community participation. A contemporary local account reported that the certification effort involved hundreds of homes along with schools and community spaces. The aim was not simply to create isolated wildlife gardens, but to build a network of habitat across the city.That distinction mattered in a place experiencing rapid residential and commercial growth. Rather than treating wildlife conservation as something limited to parks or protected land, the Johns Creek initiative brought it into ordinary neighbourhoods, where gardens, schoolyards and shared spaces could collectively provide resources for birds, insects and other wildlife.Barnard’s work also began attracting attention beyond Johns Creek. In 2011, he was named one of four finalists for Atlanta’s Cox Conserves Heroes programme. Each finalist received $1,250 to support an environmental nonprofit or project, and Barnard directed his award toward his community habitat work, including grants for school gardens.The recognition continued after Johns Creek received its certification. In 2013, Barnard won first place in the 13-to-16 age category of Action for Nature’s International Young Eco-Hero Awards for his work organising the community around wildlife habitat. More than a decade later, the initiative has not disappeared. The NWF’s current community profile lists Johns Creek as an active certified community and records its original certification in April 2012, alongside subsequent recertification efforts. The city continues to work with local conservation partners to maintain its wildlife-habitat status.What began as a young person’s idea ultimately changed the way an entire suburb approached nature. In Johns Creek, conservation did not require setting the city aside from development. Instead, it meant finding ways for wildlife and everyday community life to coexist, one garden, school and shared space at a time.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: She struggled to find a job despite a postgraduate degree and faced rejection as a transgender woman; now 36-year-old Riyana Suree helps others find sponsors, education and a place to stay in Tamil Nadu
articles.summary: A postgraduate degree, a talent for dance and the determination to build a career did not make things easier for Riyana Suree.
articles.body: A postgraduate degree, a talent for dance and the determination to build a career did not make things easier for Riyana Suree. When the transgender woman approached private companies looking for a job, her qualifications were not enough to protect her from rejection. Even people who initially showed interest in learning dance from her reportedly changed their minds after discovering that she was transgender.Today, at 36, Riyana is working to ensure that other transgender people do not have to face the same barriers alone. Through the Thiru Aval Trust, she helps transgender students find educational sponsors, offers accommodation to those who have nowhere to stay and supports people looking for employment and livelihood opportunities.Her journey from struggling to find acceptance and professional opportunities to creating them for others is a story of turning personal setbacks into a larger purpose.A postgraduate degree, but no job opportunitiesBorn in Dindigul in 1990 and raised in Tiruchy, Riyana began recognising herself as a girl when she was 12. According to The New Indian Express, her journey as a transgender woman formally began in 2006. Her father, D Soosai Sagayam, worked in the cooperative sector, while her mother, Insiya Mary, is a homemaker.Acceptance within the family took time. Initially, she was not allowed to dress as a woman during family functions. Her sister-in-law, Gayathri Lenin, played an important role in helping the family understand and accept her identity.Academically, Riyana completed her bachelor's degree in Physics from St Joseph's College in Tiruchy and went on to pursue postgraduate studies at Jamal Mohamed College. She was also passionate about dance and had won several competitions.However, when she approached two or three private companies, including firms in the IT sector, for employment in 2013, she encountered repeated rejections.The experience affected her confidence to approach other organisations. She subsequently joined the Tamil Nadu State AIDS Control Society (TANSACS) as an outreach worker under a government programme, earning Rs 8,000 a month. She continued in the role for more than eight years, supplementing her income through dance performances and teaching.But even her interest in dance came with its own challenges.“Many people initially showed interest in joining my dance classes. But once they came to know that I was a transgender woman, several backed out,” she recalled, as reported by The New Indian Express.Riyana also attempted the TNPSC Group IV and railway recruitment examinations but could not clear them.A chance encounter opened the doors to modellingAn unexpected opportunity came in 2018. A photographer came across Riyana's photographs on Facebook and approached her for a photoshoot. The pictures attracted attention and gradually opened doors to modelling assignments and beauty pageants.She participated in several competitions, including Miss Trichy, Miss Koovagam, Miss Trans Queen India and Miss South India Trans. In 2023, she won the Miss Universe Trans India title at a competition held in New Delhi.The recognition gave her a platform beyond modelling. She now mentors contestants and conducts interview sessions in her capacity as the national director.However, while her own career was finding direction, Riyana had also begun thinking about how she could make opportunities more accessible to other transgender people.From opening her home to finding sponsors for studentsRiyana started the Thiru Aval Trust in 2019, which was officially registered in 2022. During the Covid-19 pandemic, she and her associates distributed food to transgender people and others in need. Over time, the initiative expanded to include education, employment, livelihood and medical assistance. Around 30 transgender people are associated with the trust.One of its important initiatives involves connecting transgender students with sponsors who can support their education.S Sayeesha, 27, from Tiruchy, is among those who received help. With Riyana's assistance in finding a sponsor, Sayeesha completed her MSc, BEd and teacher training. However, despite attending several interviews, she has not yet been able to secure a job in a private school and is preparing for government recruitment examinations, including TNPSC.“Although my family has accepted me, coming from an orthodox Muslim background, society has not. I have completed my studies and teacher training, but finding a job remains difficult,” Sayeesha said.Riyana's support has also extended beyond financial assistance. When Joshka Jasmine, 30, from Thanjavur, came to study at Government Law College in Tiruchy but had no place to stay, Riyana offered her a home. She also helped her find sponsors for her education.Joshka, who initially aspired to become a model, eventually chose law because she wanted to work for the transgender community and improve access to justice. She has been practising for two years and affectionately calls Riyana her 'mummy'.In another significant development, Joshka and Sowmiya Shashu, 37, were recently honoured at the 2026 convocation after graduating in 2024. They were the first transgender graduates to receive the honour since the college was established in 1980, according to The New Indian Express.Joshka also highlighted the community's long-standing demand for equal opportunities in education and employment.“We have been demanding horizontal reservation for the past 15 years and urge the state government to implement it,” she said.Creating opportunities where she once struggled to find themThe trust has also experimented with livelihood initiatives. Between 2021 and 2023, it ran a restaurant that employed five transgender people. It continues to distribute surplus food from functions and provides medical assistance, including support for transgender people living with HIV.Riyana now hopes to bring more organisations into these efforts and create opportunities in creative industries. In association with Iravi Trust, she is planning an LGBTQ-themed fashion runway in Tiruchy to showcase transgender talent.For her, the motivation comes from remembering the opportunities she could not access when she was starting out.“When I did not get an opportunity, I wanted to create one for someone else. That is the thought behind our efforts through the Thiru Aval Trust to support education, employment and livelihood,” she said.And while modelling titles and pageant recognition have marked important milestones in her own journey, Riyana says the real reward lies elsewhere.“The greatest satisfaction comes from seeing someone facing challenges like mine complete their education, get a job and live with self-respect,” she said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Oprah Winfrey helped launch a $60 million disaster-relief fund for Maui wildfire survivors; in June 2026, a separate donation delivered a new CT scanner to Maui Memorial Medical Center for local patients
articles.summary: Media mogul Oprah Winfrey has continued supporting residents of Hawaii’s Maui island, where devastating wildfires destroyed homes and displaced thousands
articles.body: Media mogul Oprah Winfrey has continued supporting residents of Hawaii’s Maui island, where devastating wildfires destroyed homes and displaced thousands of people in 2023. After joining actor Dwayne Johnson to launch the People’s Fund of Maui, which ultimately distributed $60 million to wildfire survivors, Winfrey made a separate contribution to healthcare in June 2026, helping Maui Memorial Medical Center acquire a new computed tomography (CT) scanner.According to Maui Health, the hospital system’s official announcement on June 12, 2026, Winfrey’s donation to the Maui Health Foundation made the advanced imaging equipment possible. The scanner was formally blessed during a ceremony on June 8, attended by Winfrey, members of the hospital’s imaging team and local spiritual leader Kahu Kimokeo Kapahulehua. The equipment is expected to strengthen access to diagnostic services for patients across Maui County.New CT scanner aims to improve diagnosis and treatmentThe new scanner at Maui Memorial Medical Center is designed to provide faster and more detailed medical images, helping physicians identify illnesses and make treatment decisions with greater precision. CT scans use X-rays and computer processing to produce detailed images of structures inside the body, helping doctors investigate injuries and diagnose a range of medical conditions. Maui Health said the new technology would help physicians diagnose and treat patients earlier and more accurately, while strengthening access to high-quality healthcare across the island county. The hospital’s imaging department will operate the equipment as part of its diagnostic services.The June 8 ceremony included a traditional blessing led by Kapahulehua. He blessed the scanner and the hands of the caregivers who would operate it, recognising the responsibilities of the imaging team in treating patients. Winfrey also joined the hospital staff during the event, marking the installation of equipment made possible by her contribution.The hospital expressed gratitude to Winfrey and her team for supporting the community’s healthcare needs. Neither the hospital’s announcement nor the local reports cited here disclosed the monetary value of her CT scanner donation.How Oprah Winfrey and Dwayne Johnson launched a $60 million relief fundWinfrey’s latest contribution follows a major relief initiative launched after the August 2023 Maui wildfires. The fires devastated Lahaina, a historic town on the island’s western coast, and caused widespread destruction, deaths and displacement. Residents faced the immediate loss of homes and belongings, alongside the longer-term challenges of finding housing and rebuilding their lives. On August 31, 2023, Winfrey and Johnson announced the People’s Fund of Maui, initially committing $10 million of their own money and inviting others to contribute. The initiative was designed to provide direct financial assistance to adults who had been displaced by the fires in Lahaina and Kula, allowing survivors to decide how best to use the money according to their individual circumstances.Under the programme, eligible adults were offered $1,200 per month during the distribution period. Rather than restricting assistance to specific purchases, the fund gave recipients flexibility to cover expenses such as housing, bills, transport and other immediate needs.The Entertainment Industry Foundation, which administered the fund, later reported that $60 million had been distributed to more than 8,100 residents. The final amount was substantially higher than the initial $10 million commitment announced at the fund’s launch.Direct payments offered survivors flexibilityThe fund’s approach was based on the idea that people affected by a disaster should have the freedom to decide which expenses were most urgent for them. Its administrators worked with local community leaders and elders while establishing the initiative, with the aim of reaching people who had lost their homes or whose homes had become uninhabitable.An Associated Press report published in April 2024 documented how the assistance helped survivors manage expenses while dealing with the aftermath of the fires. Some recipients used the money towards mortgage payments and essential household costs, while others faced vehicle repairs and the financial pressures associated with rebuilding their lives. The report also highlighted the scale of the continuing crisis. Thousands of people had been displaced, and survivors continued to confront housing shortages, prolonged stays in temporary accommodation and the emotional toll of losing homes and community connections. The relief payments offered a measure of financial flexibility, but they could not resolve the broader challenges of recovery.A separate contribution to Maui’s healthcare needsWinfrey’s June 2026 donation to the Maui Health Foundation represents a separate form of support, focused on medical infrastructure rather than direct cash payments to wildfire survivors. The new scanner is intended to benefit patients across Maui County, not exclusively those affected by the fires.The donation also comes amid wider efforts to strengthen the island’s healthcare facilities. In September 2026, Maui Health Foundation announced that three donors had secured $4.1 million for a new MRI system at Maui Memorial Medical Center. The Oprah Winfrey Charitable Foundation contributed $500,000 towards that project, alongside funding from the Stable Road Foundation and Maui residents Nan and Wayne Kocourek.You use AI every day. articles.title: Big setback ahead of Punjab elections; 3 AAP rebel MLAs join BJP
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Three Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) leaders from Punjab, including rebel MLAs Harmeet Singh Pathanmajra and Chetan Singh Jouramajra, joined the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Three Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) leaders from Punjab, including rebel MLAs Harmeet Singh Pathanmajra and Chetan Singh Jouramajra, joined the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Monday, days after breaking ties with the Arvind Kejriwal-led party. The third leader is suspended AAP MLA and former IPS officer Kunwar Vijay Pratap Singh, who also resigned from the Punjab Assembly on Monday.Pathanmajra and Jouramajra were seen raising slogans of 'BJP zindabad' at the BJP headquarters in Delhi, according to a video shared by news agency ANI.The development comes a day after Pathanmajra, who represents the Sanour constituency, and Jouramajra, the MLA from Samana in Punjab's Patiala district, resigned from the primary membership of the AAP. Both leaders had accused the Bhagwant Mann-led government of failing to address issues such as the drug menace, rising state debt and governance-related concerns.Their exits came shortly after the AAP released its first list of 40 candidates for the 2027 Punjab Assembly elections. Neither Sanour nor Samana figured in the list.AAP had said it would approach the Punjab Assembly Speaker seeking cancellation of the legislative membership of both MLAs, alleging that they had engaged in anti-party activities. The party had suspended both leaders before they announced their resignations.Kunwar Vijay Pratap Singh resigns as Punjab MLAThe political developments also saw suspended AAP MLA and former IPS officer Kunwar Vijay Pratap Singh resign from the Punjab Assembly. Singh, who represents Amritsar North, submitted his resignation to assembly Speaker Kultar Singh Sandhwan.In a Facebook post, Singh announced his decision, stating, "I have resigned from the membership of Punjab Vidhan Sabha."In his resignation letter to the Speaker, he wrote, "I hereby tender my resignation of my seat in the House with effect from 1.11.2026."Singh was suspended from the AAP for five years in June 2025 over alleged anti-party activities. His suspension followed his criticism of the Punjab Vigilance Bureau's action against Shiromani Akali Dal leader Bikram Singh Majithia.A former member of the Punjab Police special investigation team (SIT) that probed the 2015 Kotkapura and Behbal Kalan police-firing incidents, Singh had repeatedly questioned the Mann government's handling of the sacrilege cases.AAP targets BJP over induction of rebel leadersThe BJP's induction of the rebel AAP leaders has drawn criticism from the ruling party in Punjab. Punjab AAP president Aman Arora accused the BJP of attempting to induct leaders who had left or been expelled from other parties.AAP chief spokesperson Kuldeep Singh Dhaliwal had also described the BJP as a 'kabaad di dukaan' (scrap shop), accusing it of collecting rejected political faces.Before announcing his resignation, Pathanmajra had said that the two leaders would join a party that worked in the interest of Punjab.Jouramajra, a former Punjab minister, served in the Bhagwant Mann cabinet from January 2023 to September 2024 before being dropped during a cabinet reshuffle.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Shakira's Barefoot Foundation has supported over 224,000 disadvantaged children, with 8 in 10 graduates pursuing higher education; its funding is building schools, training teachers and supporting Indigenous communities
articles.summary: Shakira's Barefoot Foundation has supported more than 224,000 children and young people in Colombia, helping expand access to education through school
articles.body: Shakira's Barefoot Foundation has supported more than 224,000 children and young people in Colombia, helping expand access to education through school construction, teacher training and educational programmes. Founded by the Colombian singer in 1997, Fundación Pies Descalzos works with communities facing economic and social barriers to quality education. The organisation reports that 8 in 10 students graduating from its supported schools continue to higher education, compared with approximately four in 10 young people nationally. Its work also includes improving educational facilities in underserved areas, providing school supplies and supporting Indigenous communities.Shakira's foundation focuses on education as a path out of inequalityShakira established Fundación Pies Descalzos in 1997 to help children in Colombia access quality education. The organisation, also known as the Barefoot Foundation, focuses on children and young people in vulnerable communities, where financial difficulties and limited educational infrastructure can restrict opportunities.Rather than concentrating exclusively on school construction, the foundation combines infrastructure projects with teacher training, educational support and programmes intended to help students continue their studies.Its approach also involves working with public schools and local communities to improve learning environments. According to the foundation, its projects aim to ensure that children can develop the knowledge and skills needed to pursue further education and build better prospects for themselves and their families.Eight in 10 graduates continue to higher educationOne of the foundation's most notable reported outcomes is the proportion of students who continue their education after graduating from its supported schools.According to its official impact page, eight in 10 graduates from Pies Descalzos schools continue to higher education. The foundation contrasts this with the national picture, citing data from Colombia's National Administrative Department of Statistics (DANE) indicating that approximately four in 10 young people continue to this level of education.In a November 2025 publication, the foundation said between 70% and 80% of students graduating from schools it supports continue into tertiary education. This includes technical, technological and university-level programmes.Building schools in underserved communitiesImproving access to educational infrastructure is a central part of the foundation's work. Its projects include constructing new schools and upgrading existing facilities in areas where children face barriers to quality education.In 2024, the foundation reported supporting 28,157 students across 24 Colombian municipalities through educational and school-infrastructure projects. This was in addition to approximately 6,700 children and young people enrolled in schools supported by the organisation and bearing its name.One of its projects that year was a new school in the Villas de Aranjuez neighbourhood of Cartagena. The facility was designed to serve approximately 1,000 students annually, helping expand educational provision in the area.The foundation also worked with Colombia's Ministry of National Education to improve two schools in Riohacha and Uribia, in the department of La Guajira. These projects focused on strengthening educational access for communities that include Indigenous students and migrants.Supporting Indigenous Wayúu students and migrant familiesIn 2024, the organisation and Colombia's Ministry of National Education completed interventions at two schools in Riohacha and Uribia. The facilities served more than 1,500 students, most of whom belonged to the Wayúu Indigenous community or were migrants from Venezuela.The projects used an ethno-educational approach, recognising the importance of cultural context in education. This is particularly relevant for Indigenous communities, where education programmes must account for local identities and circumstances.Training teachers and providing learning materialsThe foundation also invests in teachers, recognising that educational facilities alone cannot guarantee effective learning.Its official impact figures report that more than 12,824 teachers have received training, with women accounting for 85% of those trained. The organisation says these programmes are intended to strengthen teaching practices and help educators introduce new skills into their classrooms.In 2024, the foundation reported that 690 teachers participated in its training programmes.The organisation also distributed 10,965 kits, uniforms and reading materials to students, teachers, school leaders and coordinators that year. Such supplies can help schools and families meet some of the practical requirements of education.These initiatives complement the foundation's infrastructure projects by supporting the people and resources involved in students' day-to-day learning.Foundation reports more than 282,000 beneficiariesAlthough the foundation's impact page reports that it has supported more than 224,000 children and young people, its English-language homepage now lists a higher cumulative figure.The homepage reports more than 282,160 children and young people benefited, over 13,387 teachers trained and more than 300 public schools supported in Colombia. It also lists 22 schools built or improved in Colombia, two in Haiti and one in Soweto.The foundation also reports working with 1,131 families and caregivers, 80% of whom are women, according to its impact page. This highlights another dimension of its work: involving families in supporting children's development and education.Shakira's foundation expands support beyond the classroomThe organisation's work has also extended into partnerships intended to help young people navigate education and prepare for their futures.In April 2026, Colombia's student-loan and educational-support agency ICETEX announced a three-year partnership with Fundación Pies Descalzos under its Comunidad ICETEX project.The collaboration aims to support young people as they prepare for higher education, continue their studies and move towards employment. Its planned areas of work include financial education, emotional wellbeing, career guidance, gender equality, entrepreneurship, leadership and employability.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran killed her teenage daughter - now she is facing up to the regime
articles.summary: Samira's 16-year-old daughter Sevda was shot dead as they took part in mass protests in January.
articles.body:
Warning: Distressing content and strong language

Samira says she never used to be political.

"I worked in sales in Iran. I sold cosmetics," she tells BBC Panorama.

But that all changed the day her only child was shot dead in front of her by Iranian security forces. Sixteen-year-old Sevda was taking part in protests against Iran's repressive regime that engulfed the country earlier this year - before the US and Israel launched widespread air strikes which killed the country's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Samira's grief became fury as Iran's authorities then hindered, rather than helped, her search for her daughter's body, she says.

"I realised that finding Sevda wasn't the end, but just the beginning of all the harassment they put me through."

Samira made a dramatic escape from Iran on foot, navigating dangerous mountainous terrain.

She now lives abroad in hiding, describing herself as a "one-woman army fighting the regime". In a search for accountability and justice after her daughter's death, she is intent on naming the members of the security forces and officials she believes were responsible for firing fatal shots during the protests.

"They'll bring me to the brink of death before they kill me, but finding me won't be easy… Return to normal life? There is no going back," she says.

Samira is among several Iranians the BBC has spoken to since the start of the year. Some, still inside the country, told Panorama they wanted to speak out despite the risks, saying they had found it difficult to hold on to hope once the mass protests had been brutally crushed.

The Iranian embassy in London told Panorama that peaceful and legitimate protests had been hijacked by foreign powers, including the US, which promoted violence, provided weapons and equipment, and compromised public security.

Sevda was killed on 9 January as she and Samira took part in huge demonstrations on the outskirts of the capital Tehran which had begun the previous month. They had been sparked by economic discontent, before escalating into calls for an end to the country's Islamic Republic.

Though Samira denies she was especially political then, she says her daughter was. Sevda's idols were two other young women - Mahsa Amini, whose death in custody after an alleged violation against the mandatory headscarf triggered mass protests, and Nika Shakarami, who was killed during a subsequent uprising against Iran's strict Islamic dress code for women.

"She kept them alive in her thoughts and always wanted to continue their path [of resistance]," Samira says.

The day before Sevda was killed, the numbers protesting had been particularly high. Samira says she and Sevda had responded to a call by Reza Pahlavi , the exiled son of Iran's last shah (king), for demonstrations.

"The security forces had lost control," she says.

The swell in numbers had spooked Iran's government, and the following day a shoot-to-kill order was announced, Samira says. But she had thought it just an empty threat.

"They lied so much in Iran… We couldn't imagine a massacre of that scale."

And they were reassured, she says, by US President Trump's promise that he had their backs.

He had told US media on 8 January: "I have let [the Iranian authorities] know that if they start killing people, which they tend to do during their riots… we're going to hit them very hard."

But nevertheless the crowds appeared smaller on the 9th, Samira says.

Sevda seemed to know the risks, she says. Her daughter took off her earrings and gave them to her grandmother. She also shared her phone passcode with Samira.

The mother and daughter gathered with the rest of the protesters. Sevda then stood on a dustbin and began leading a chant.

"It seemed there were more forces than people," Samira says of the area where they were. "I don't know how, within one day, they gathered so many… Basijis and IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] forces."

The IRGC defends the country's Islamic establishment , and the paramilitary Basij Resistance Force are volunteers for the IRGC.

"A sniper fired from the roof of a building on our right. The bullet must have come from the rooftop. The bullet went through her heart. I couldn't even scream. I just stared at Sevda - her body lying lifeless. Blood was gushing out her mouth and nose. I couldn't believe it, I couldn't believe she was dying. Her eyes were still looking at me."

Samira says she managed to get Sevda to hospital and she was told they were operating on her, but then the door opened and she saw Sevda had been zipped into a body bag.

Sevda's body was taken away. Samira says it took her days to find her daughter again. Like many others, she found herself at one of Tehran's largest morgues.

"Teenagers - young boys and girls. So many had been killed," she cries.

"I died with every bag I unzipped. I'd never seen so many bodies. But I wouldn't give up."

She finally found her daughter. "Three bodies were piled on top of Sevda. That's how we found her."

Iranian authorities acknowledge that more than 3,000 people were killed in the protests, but claim some were members of the security forces. One human rights group, Hrana, however, estimates the number of dead stands at more than 7,000, most of them protesters.

Finding Sevda's body was just the beginning of Samira's battle with the authorities, she says.

To be allowed to take away the body for burial, she says she was forced to say that "terrorists" rather than the security forces had been responsible for Sevda's death.

"They did this to cover up what they'd done on 8 and 9 January, to hide how many people they had killed. They silenced families by telling them to say their loved ones were killed by Israeli or American terrorists."

Nevertheless she was barred from visiting the grave after the funeral, or organising a tombstone, she says.

And Samira says the harassment continued. A few days before the ceremony to mark 40 days since Sevda died - highly significant in Iranian culture - she says she was summoned by a local branch of the Ministry of Intelligence.

"They told me: 'You should give us an interview and say that Sevda was a Basiji and she was killed by the protesters. Then we will announce her [as] a martyr - you will then receive perks, a house, or anything that you want.'"

She is sure this offer was prompted by fear, because she had shared Sevda's death with an Iranian media organisation based in London, once the internet had been reconnected in the country.

"It scared them that I was in touch with external networks or those outside Iran."

To avoid giving the interview, Samira fled Iran as soon as the 40th day anniversary was over.

"I didn't want to trade with my child's blood."

She says people smugglers helped her to escape. She crossed rivers and mountains to get to safety.

A video she made of herself fleeing makes clear her fury.

"This crap government, these bastards, they've harassed me so much," she tells the camera as she marches along a mountain path bordered by a deep ravine.

Samira says after she continued to give interviews to foreign media from abroad, she was charged in absentia with a string of offences, including "moharebeh" - waging war against God - which can carry the death penalty.

To mark what would have been Sevda's 17th birthday, her relatives and friends held a vigil - with Samira watching from exile on a livestream.

"Then suddenly, the feed cut out," she says.

She discovered that the event had been raided, she says, and some of her family and friends arrested by the IRGC.

She says her family was warned by the authorities that, if they continued to gather at Sevda's grave, her body would be exhumed and moved elsewhere.

Now, Samira shares the names, online, of Iranian security force members and officials she believes were responsible for firing fatal shots during the 8 and 9 January protests she and Sevda joined.

"I want justice to be served for every single person whose name I expose, because they have killed so many young people. My goal is for them to be identified so they can be put on trial," she says.

When one of the men Samira named online was later found dead, a regime supporter offered a $5,000 (£3,732) reward for information about her whereabouts, presuming she was responsible. Iranian state media has since reported the arrest of nine people in connection with the death.

Despite the risks, Samira says she refuses to be silenced.

"Every day and every second without Sevda is very difficult for me. It's like a mother who has lost her heart, who has lost her being, has lost her life…

"But the fact that Sevda is not breathing has made it possible for me to stand on my feet… to think about honouring her life and her path... all those bodies I saw, all those body bags I opened looking for Sevda, they all made me fight the Islamic Republic until my last breath."

articles.title: UN staffer’s death in custody exposes Houthi ‘political extortion’ in Yemen
articles.summary: Following a UN staffer’s death, rights experts expose systematic abuses and demand international accountability in Yemen
articles.body:
The United Nations is demanding a thorough investigation into the death of a human rights employee while in Houthi detention in Yemen.

Mohammad el-Shami , who worked for the UN Human Rights Office, died more than a month ago but his family was only recently notified. He had been arbitrarily detained by the rebel group, which controls much of northern Yemen, since June 2024.

His death has highlighted the number of UN and NGO workers targeted by the Houthis, since they captured the capital Sanaa in September 2014.

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk has urged the Houthi authorities in Sanaa to ensure a prompt, transparent and independent investigation into el-Shami’s death.

“This is a heartbreaking loss for the UN Human Rights Office and the wider United Nations. Mohammad’s family has not received any explanation of the cause or circumstances of his death – they deserve to know the truth,” said Turk.

“This requires disclosure of all relevant medical and detention records, preservation of evidence and independent scrutiny of any stated cause of death. There must be accountability for wrongdoing.”

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also expressed his dismay and demanded the immediate release of all detained personnel.

“I am appalled & deeply saddened by the death of a @UN colleague, Mohammad el Shami, while in the custody of the Houthi de facto authorities in Yemen,” Guterres stated.

“I remain gravely concerned for the safety & wellbeing of the UN personnel, former UN staff & personnel from humanitarian & civil society organisations who remain detained. I reiterate my call for their immediate & unconditional release.”

The Houthis have repeatedly accused detained workers of being spies.

The Houthis accused more than 60 UN and NGO workers detained in 2024, when el-Shami was arrested, of being part of an “American-Israeli spy network”.

The group has routinely arrested civil rights activists, NGO workers and other civilians on espionage allegations.

As of February this year, 73 UN staff and dozens of other humanitarian workers were in detention, according to Amnesty International . El-Shami is the second UN staff member to die in Houthi custody, following the death of a World Food Programme employee in February 2025.

The Minister of Human Rights for Yemen’s internationally recognised government, Meshdal Mohammed, held the militia fully responsible for el-Shami’s abduction, forced disappearance and death.

“The continued abduction of [civil rights workers] for more than two years, culminating in the announcement of the death of one of them without enabling his family to visit him or know his condition, dictates a serious review of the way this file is handled,” he said.

Local human rights advocates highlight the severe difficulty of achieving accountability for deaths and other civil rights abuses by the Houthis.

Tawfik Alhamidi, President of SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties, outlined the systematic obstacles faced by NGO workers operating in Houthi-controlled territories in Yemen.

“The group is the one that controls prisons, medical records and witnesses, in addition to the fact that there is no judicial or human rights oversight over places of detention,” he told Al Jazeera.

“This delay by this group and the withholding of information may reflect a systematic pattern or behaviour by this group, at least in order perhaps to hide some features or make it difficult to conduct an examination.”

He said that the deaths of many Yemenis in Houthi custody have been put down to disease, sudden death or suicide.

The Houthi authorities remain fully accountable for any deaths in custody, regardless of the exact cause, Alhamidi added.

“Even if illness is proven, the question remains: Did the detainee also receive medical care, or is there negligence or is there deprivation?”

articles.title: Meet Emily Herra, 17-year-old New York student who helped turn a neglected 3,600-square-foot lot into a community garden with pollinator habitat and a 130-foot mural, then won a $10,000 prize in 2026
articles.summary: When Emily Herra was 12, she tried to introduce a composting programme at her school.
articles.body: When Emily Herra was 12, she tried to introduce a composting programme at her school. The idea was met with resistance from administrators who believed it would be too complicated to implement. But the young New Yorker persisted, eventually getting the programme running and setting her sights on a bigger challenge: transforming a neglected patch of land in her neighbourhood into a space where people and nature are now thriving together.Five years later, the now 17-year-old has been recognised for her environmental work with the 2026 Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes. She co-founded Veggie Nuggets, a youth-led climate activism group based in Jackson Heights and the wider Queens area of New York City. Its signature project is the restoration of a previously abandoned 3,600-square-foot lot, which now features 1,800 square feet of pollinator habitat and a 130-foot climate justice mural.The prize, announced on September 15, 2026, recognises young people who have made a significant positive difference to their communities or the environment. Herra is among 15 top winners, each receiving $10,000 to support their service work or higher education, according to the award's official announcement.From school composting to a neighbourhood gardenHerra's environmental work began with a relatively simple idea: making better use of waste. After getting the composting programme at her school off the ground, she wanted to extend her efforts beyond the campus.The opportunity came when she and her friends encountered an abandoned strip of land in Jackson Heights. The site, along 69th Street beside the CSX railway tracks, was covered in overgrown vegetation and rubbish. It was here the students saw an opportunity to create something useful for their community.A group of seven middle school students returned to clean up the area, working alongside two coaches. With guidance from master gardeners and the Jackson Heights Beautification Group, they learnt how to improve the soil and introduce native plants.The transformation required more than gardening skills. The young volunteers also had to navigate permits, applications and funding processes to secure the resources needed to maintain the space. Their work gradually turned the neglected patch into a community garden where residents could volunteer, learn about the environment and help support local biodiversity.The garden now contains a substantial pollinator habitat and a mural measuring 130 feet. The project combines environmental restoration with public art, using the space to draw attention to climate justice while creating a welcoming neighbourhood gathering point.When the garden disappeared overnightThe project did not develop without setbacks. In autumn 2024, a contractor hired by CSX cleared the strip of land, apparently unaware that the students had established a garden there. Much of their work was wiped out. In a report by The Indypendent, Herra described the destruction as one of the most difficult moments the group had experienced together. The loss threatened not only the plants and garden beds they had built, but also the time and effort the young volunteers had invested in the site.The group, however, decided to rebuild rather than abandon the project. Veggie Nuggets subsequently secured a lease with CSX, giving it recognised permission to work on the land and reducing the risk of the garden being accidentally cleared again. The group also received a grant of approximately $10,000 to purchase tools, rebuild beds, install signs and replace plants.Herra shared that the rebuilding process was still underway while she and her teammates were watching the garden return gradually, even though the work was not yet complete.The entire experience became more than just an initiative. It was the subject of 'Perennial', a documentary made by members of Veggie Nuggets. The film premiered at the Queens World Film Festival on November 8, 2025, documenting the group's response to the destruction and its efforts to restore the space.More than planting treesVeggie Nuggets' work extends beyond one single garden. The group organises park clean-ups, environmental workshops and community activities while advocating for sustainable practices such as composting and renewable energy. Its members have also participated in campaigns against fossil-fuel infrastructure.The organisation describes itself as a youth climate activism group working to improve neighbourhoods in Jackson Heights and Astoria. articles.title: Short of space, the Guggenheim sold a Kandinsky for $62,000. It may fetch $80 million at auction
articles.summary: Collector Solomon R. Guggenheim’s foundation once sold off 50 Wassily Kandinsky paintings “for want of space.” Decades later, one is poised to smash auction records.
articles.body: Some 15 years after Solomon R. Guggenheim died, the foundation managing his extensive art collection concluded that it owned more Wassily Kandinsky paintings than it knew what to do with. The late American businessman had been among the Russian painter’s most prominent and dedicated patrons. But in 1964, despite operating its namesake museum in Manhattan, Guggenheim’s foundation placed 50 of its 170 Kandinsky works — characteristically colorful, geometric takes on abstraction — on sale “for want of space.” Announcing the decision, his nephew, Harry F. Guggenheim, said trustees feared the art would otherwise remain hidden away “in our vaults,” according to reports at the time. “We have concluded that this should not be the fate of these paintings,” he added. It was a noble sentiment but perhaps, in hindsight, a costly one. At a London auction later that year, the 50 paintings fetched a combined £536,580, then equivalent to around $1.5 million. Many of them have since reappeared on the market at significantly higher prices. And now one of the works — “Betonte Ecken,” which in 1964 attracted a winning bid of just £22,000 (then around $62,000, or $540,000 in today’s money) from a New York art dealer — is returning to auction with an estimate of $60 million to $80 million. “The Guggenheim had such an embarrassment of riches back then,” said Max Carter, global chairman of 20th and 21st century art at Christie’s, the auction house behind this month’s sale. The foundation “sold tremendous masterpieces, which would be unthinkable to sell today,” he added, speaking over the phone from New York. “Betonte Ecken” is not just poised to break the auction record for Kandinsky’s work — it is certain to do so. Christie’s said a guarantor has confirmed an offer exceeding the record £37.2 million ($44.55 million) paid for his painting “Murnau mit Kirche II” in 2023. The dramatic appreciation in the value of Kandinsky’s work is a testament to his status in today’s art market. While his reputation was well-established by the time of the Guggenheim sale (at which point he had already been dead for two decades), “Betonte Ecken” was, then, “still very forward-looking,” Carter said. “Now it’s become canonical,” he added, calling the painting “quintessential” Kandinsky. “If you were to go on the street and ask the first 10 people who’d heard of Kandinsky to close their eyes and describe what one of his masterpieces looked like, it would be this.” Color, complexity, composition A major figure in the emergence of abstraction in the 1910s, Kandinsky painted “Betonte Ecken” between December 1922 and January 1923. It is a key period in the artist’s career — and the abstract movement at large — that is responsible for some of his most sought-after works. Following a seven-year stint in his native Russia, Kandinsky had just returned to Germany, where he lived before the outbreak of World War I. His art had increasingly clashed with the anti-bourgeois ideology of the new Soviet regime (he would also later be branded a degenerate by the Nazis), so he accepted an invitation to teach theory at the famous Bauhaus school in Weimar. Painted shortly after his arrival, “Betonte Ecken” typifies Kandinsky’s highly theoretical approach to form and geometry. Its complexity, color and composition all “synthesize everything that came before it,” Carter said. “For some collectors, this is his greatest and most important period,” he added. The painting also speaks to the influential role of music in Kandinsky’s oeuvre. He famously chose an art career after attending a Wagner concert at Moscow’s Bolshoi Theatre in 1896. (“I saw all my colors in my mind; they stood before my eyes,” he later wrote of the experience. “Wild, almost crazy lines were sketched in front of me”). As well as featuring black lines resembling those of a musical score, “Betonte Ecken” is also “symphonic” in a less literal sense, Carter said. “When you stand in front of this painting, the relation of all of these disparate shapes and elements — which in the hands of an inferior artist would be chaotic and jumbled and perhaps incoherent — are extremely harmonious,” he said, adding: “It’s really about the relations of the forms to one another.” Painted on a square canvas more than 4.25 feet tall and wide, “Betonte Ecken” (which is German for “Emphasized Corners”) is unusually large for a Kandinsky. The relative rarity of his work has also influenced its value, said Carter. Compared to his contemporaries, Kandinsky was not especially prolific. While there is no exact figure for his output, one catalogue raisonné — a scholarly compendium of an artist’s known works — lists fewer than 1,200 oil paintings. (By contrast, one of Pablo Picasso’s catalogues raisonnés contains more than 16,000 paintings and drawings.) Of these, many are housed by institutions that would, now, never dream of selling them. Among them, still, is the Guggenheim, which has since acquired new Kandinsky works and currently owns more than 150. The museum may have lost millions of dollars’ worth of masterpieces from its balance sheet, but it arguably retained its most iconic examples, including the famous “Komposition VIII.” As the great collector’s nephew said ahead of the 1964 sale, the foundation only auctioned off paintings that could “reasonably be released without diminishing the standing of the museum’s permanent collection.”

articles.title: Anthrax outbreak kills hippos in DR Congo’s Virunga National Park
articles.summary: Drought and conflict compound the threat to wildlife in eastern DR Congo.
articles.body:
Vitshumbi, DR Congo – While the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to grapple with the deadliest Ebola outbreak in its history, another disease is taking a heavy toll on wildlife in Virunga National Park in the country’s east.

Over the past four weeks, hippopotamus carcasses have been discovered in the Semuliki River, west of Africa’s oldest national park, raising concern among communities living along its banks.

“It was in mid-September that we began to notice the mass deaths of hippos in the Semuliki River. We have started to fear this situation, which is unfolding whilst we are in the midst of the Ebola outbreak,” Michael Kambale, a resident of the Vitshumbi enclave, about 100 kilometres (62 miles) north of Goma, the capital of North Kivu province, told Al Jazeera.

Following laboratory tests, Virunga National Park confirmed that anthrax, caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis, was responsible for the wildlife deaths.

According to park officials, 28 hippos died over approximately one month.

“This disease can be transmitted to humans through contact with a dead or sick animal or by consuming its meat,” Virunga National Park said in a press release sent to Al Jazeera.

Anthrax threatens wildlife and local communities

Joel Mbusa Mapoli, an expert in ecology and veterinary medicine, said the deaths represented a significant loss for Virunga National Park and called for urgent action to contain the outbreak.

He explained that hippos act as ecosystem engineers, altering nutrient flows and the ecological conditions of their habitats.

Virunga National Park said it was focusing on surveillance, the safe management of carcasses and reducing risks to wildlife and local communities.

“Teams are monitoring the affected area, recording new cases of mortality and coordinating the safe handling and disposal of carcasses,” the park said.

“People living in the affected area and its surroundings are being informed about the outbreak; they are advised not to touch, skin or consume animals found dead, and to report any carcasses or suspected cases to the relevant authorities,” the park added.

Founded in 1925, Virunga is Africa’s oldest national park and is renowned for its biodiversity.

Olivier Ndoole Bahemuke, a Congolese environmental activist and head of Alerte Congolaise pour l’environnement et les droits de l’homme, a nonprofit organisation operating in the DRC, said the armed conflict that has persisted in the country for nearly three decades had fuelled poaching and deforestation.

The park says it has lost control of a significant part of its territory over the past four years because of the ongoing conflict between the Congolese army and M23 fighters.

The M23 armed group says it is helping protect the area from poachers and other potential human threats.

Park officials said anthrax outbreaks had previously been observed among hippos and other wild animals in the ecosystem during periods of drought.

According to Mapoli, several factors contribute to recurring anthrax outbreaks in Virunga National Park. These include the persistence of the bacterium in the environment, deteriorating ecological and climatic conditions, the concentration of animals around aquatic habitats and difficulties in monitoring wildlife health.

“When vegetation becomes scarce, herbivores may graze closer to the ground and congregate around the few remaining grazing areas and water points, thereby increasing their exposure to contaminated soil,” Virunga National Park said in a statement sent to Al Jazeera, adding that the situation was being monitored “closely”.

The park’s February 2026 census estimated the hippo population at more than 2,700, distributed across 171 groups.

In 2025, an anthrax outbreak killed 65 hippos in Virunga National Park, according to the park’s February 2026 population update. Park staff mobilised excavators to retrieve the carcasses from the water.

According to park officials, anthrax can survive for decades in the soil in the form of spores.

Protecting hippos means protecting the ecosystem

Mapoli said the response to anthrax should combine conservation measures with public health interventions, in line with the One Health principle, an approach that recognises the links between human, animal and environmental health.

He called for stronger epidemiological surveillance, better protection for local communities, proper management of animal carcasses and greater collaboration among state, non-state and para-state bodies.

“The hippopotamus is one of the flagship species of the Virunga ecosystems. Its disappearance could lead to a major disruption of aquatic ecosystems, as these animals play a role in the exchange of matter between terrestrial and aquatic environments,” he told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Dakota Johnson wants you to have better sex
articles.summary: Maude founder Éva Goicochea and her co-creative director Dakota Johnson talk about sex toys in the Louvre, Shere Hite being run out of America and why we might need a Miss Rachel for sex ed.
articles.body: We live in a world that won’t stop reminding us that people have a lot to learn when it comes to sex. The news is filled with disturbing stories of sexual violence and, while it rarely makes headlines, everyday misogyny exists in our schools, workplaces and homes. Maude, the purveyor of aesthetically pleasing, elegantly designed vibrators, condoms, candles and lube, isn’t going to fix these systemic, largely patriarchal, problems. But the intimacy brand is focused on making people think about sex as a form of health and wellness, starting from inside our bedrooms (or wherever one chooses to enjoy themselves). And every little helps, maybe? I spoke with Maude’s founder Éva Goicochea and her co-creative director, the actor Dakota Johnson, about sex toys in the Louvre, Shere Hite being run out of America and why we might need a Miss Rachel for sex ed. The following conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Fiona: How did the two of you meet and decide to make it official? Dakota: I was on the verge of launching my own sort of sexual wellness brand, but I didn’t really know where to begin. There are so many sexual wellness brands that I find to be incredibly offensive and tacky and really kind of diminishing, especially towards female sexuality. So they brought Maude to my attention and then I wanted to talk to Éva and we really, really got along and I learned so much from her. Fiona: Your products are in big retailers like Target and Ulta Beauty. Two of your vibrators were also included in a museum exhibition — at the Louvre, no less! That’s certainly one way to insert yourself into cultural conversation. But I assume it also says a lot about the suave aesthetics of Maude. Why was it important to move away from the comedy dildo? Dakota: Ha! Éva: Great design is a language and it creates the potential for, in this case, destigmatization. Fiona: It’s hard to ignore the backdrop to which we’re having this conversation about sexual education and wellness — just in the last month, we’ve seen the stories of sexual violence coming out of Cornell University, the Russel Brand trial that’s ongoing here in the UK. Dakota: Sexual violence and misconduct has been occurring since the beginning of time. So I think now it’s about the people who are victims of that feeling like they can speak honestly without being like sent to the guillotine. Humanity is both incredibly advanced and evolved and deeply stunted. There are cycles, it’s like two steps forward, five steps back, and I just think that if we can create a place where people are supported to talk about their experiences and, and get also access to education and help… I think it’s about building a safer conversation around the topic. Éva: We have a lot of customers who write us to say they’ve been victims of sexual violence. Some of them just haven’t been ready to think about this part of their lives, and they’re like, ‘Thank you for existing, the products you make don’t make me feel uncomfortable, they are so neutral, I don’t feel ashamed anymore.’ Fiona: That’s powerful feedback to receive. I’m thinking about women later in life, too, a time when many women might feel like, ‘Well, I’m just not going to do that anymore! My sexual years are over.’ Éva: We get taught for maybe one to two hours, especially in the US, in school when we’re teenagers, and then we become ill-equipped to have these conversations about intimacy later in life. We wanted to be there throughout your adult life because the truth is we’re educating ourselves at every point. And Dakota, I’m not sure if you want to mention this, but I thought it was so powerful that you were involved the documentary “The disappearance of Shere Hite,” because she championed what was really happening with people and intimacy so early on. (Shere Hite was a pioneering and outspoken sexual educator known for the groundbreaking 1976 study, The Hite Report: A Nationwide Study of Female Sexuality, which surveyed thousands of American women about their sex lives. Her challenges to traditional patriarchal ideas of sex, including the revelation that roughly 70% of women were unable to achieve orgasm through penetrative intercourse, received a huge amount of backlash and upset many fragile men.) Dakota: Yeah, and she was publicly so silenced and so devalued for that. My production company TeaTime produced that documentary and I narrated it. I wasn’t even aware of the book, but my mom was and so many people in her generation and friends of hers who I would talk to were. She was such a fabulous woman. So strong… she was so cool and chic, and she was just telling the truth, and she was basically run out of America! Fiona: What other films or books do you think we have out there that are good, in terms of building a healthy sexual education? Dakota: To be honest, I haven’t really seen much. I guess you know that show “Sex Education” was good but also lacking like basic information about sex, like what you want your kids to learn when they start to understand what that is. Éva and I have talked about sex ed in schools and now like that’s not really even a thing anymore, is it Éva? Éva: Barely. Dakota: They’ve taken it out of schools. There’s not really a conversation around sex, which is such a huge issue because human beings are sexual by nature, and a human is going to have sexual urges at some point in their life. If they’re not educated, then that leads to the kind of behavior that we were talking about earlier, where it’s more aggressive, it’s more violent, it’s like something where you don’t understand where it’s coming from and how to identify with it. But in my line of work, I truly cannot give you an example. Fiona: The other way to help people talk about sex is to make it fun, and to even make it funny? One film that got me thinking about sex in a different way recently is Olivia Colman’s new film “Wicker” with Alexander Skarsgård. Dakota: I haven’t seen that yet! But even in Alex’s other movie “Pillion,” there’s a more subversive conversation about sexual discovery and something that’s really quite beautiful, even if it’s a niche pocket of sexuality. So, yes, there is a way to do this in film, but then, do you think that there’s a disconnect between people watching a narrative scripted story and then going back to their own lives? I don’t know, does there need to be like a Miss Rachel for sex ed??

articles.title: Fake alerts warn of nuclear danger as Ukraine and Russia report emergency app hacks
articles.summary: Nuclear danger, radiation threat and street combat: Ukrainians received a wave of messages Sunday night that raised alarm with a series of grave — and baseless — warnings.
articles.body: Nuclear danger, radiation threat and street combat: Ukrainians received a wave of messages Sunday night that raised alarm with a series of grave — and baseless — warnings. Authorities said the country’s emergency alert application had been targeted in a cyberattack, and hours later Russia said its own alert system had also been hacked. The dueling accusations came just as a rare humanitarian ceasefire between the two sides ended, raising fears of intensified fighting rather than a move toward broader peace. Residents in Ukraine have become used to the unsettling alerts that buzz their phones with news of incoming Russian missiles and drones — a service millions rely on to seek shelter before the attacks hit their cities. But the warnings Sunday night immediately stood out. The messages, which began around 10:45 p.m. Kyiv time (3:45 p.m. ET), warned residents not to go outside because of radiation hazard, chemical threat and street fights. Another message professed, in Russian, that all of Ukraine was under nuclear alert. “Don’t worry,” it added. “Oreshnik is in action,” referring to Russia’s nuclear-capable hypersonic missile. That message referenced a Telegram channel called Hitcorecorp. Major pro-Kremlin Telegram channel Mash said it spoke with the group and that it took responsibility for the hack. NBC News could not verify who the group is and whether it was responsible for the alerts. Shortly after the alerts went out late Sunday, Ukraine’s air force said the country’s “Air Alert” app had likely been “compromised by the enemy,” confirming there was no “radiation threat” and urging calm. In separate statements, the app’s creators said “unauthorized third parties interfered with the operation of the app,” forcing them to temporarily suspend its operations. It later called the incident a “cyberattack,” saying it was gradually restoring the service. “The team is carrying out additional measures to protect the app in order to prevent similar situations in the future,” one of the statements said. Ukrainian media reported that users across the country received the alert, and authorities in the western Lviv region reported that some of the public warning sirens and loudspeaker systems broadcast a “radiation hazard” signal. Still, many Ukrainians did not appear unduly alarmed or panicked by the alerts. In fact, many shared memes online, poking fun at what they saw as a blatant fake, and the fact the warning was issued in Russian. “No one was particularly surprised,” one user wrote on X. “They might as well have thrown in a dinosaur attack, too.” The state emergency service of Ukraine said Monday the national alert system was operating normally, and an NBC News producer in Kyiv did not experience any further issues with the “Air Alert” app. Meanwhile, Russia’s emergencies ministry also said early Monday that its mobile application has suffered a “massive cyberattack,” resulting in what it said was “dissemination of fake information to the public.” The public alert system was restored and was operating normally, it said shortly after. It emphasized that the app was only “an additional, supplementary information service.” Screenshots shared by Russian media and some regional authorities suggested the alert, issued in Russian, warned of “nuclear warheads” launched at Russia. As with the Ukrainian alert, the wording was casual and did not appear official. Russian authorities did not say who was to blame for the alleged cyberattack, only saying “malicious actors” were behind it. It was not immediately clear whether the two incidents were linked. It came just hours after a temporary ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow came to an end in the occupied southern Ukrainian region of Kherson. The truce, brokered with involvement from first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, held without violations from either side for six days, allowing the evacuation of hundreds of residents from the frontline town of Oleshky, which had been on the brink of a humanitarian catastrophe. The truce amounted to the biggest de-escalation between Kyiv and Moscow since the war started in early 2022. “On behalf of America, I commend Russia and Ukraine for their leadership and cooperation surrounding the Oleshky ceasefire,” Melania Trump said in a post on X on Sunday. “I hope Oleshky serves as a foundation for lasting peace between both nations.” Ukraine’s ombudsman ​for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, said he was exploring opportunities for “further humanitarian initiatives” with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, adding that it was “important to maintain this mechanism of cooperation.” Before the truce took hold, the United Nations estimated that some 2,000 civilians remained in Oleshky, many experiencing hunger and unable to leave safely because of heavily mined roads. Neither side has disclosed the exact number of people evacuated, but the first lady said Sunday it was nearly 800. The evacuees could go into territory controlled by either Ukraine or Russia, or remain in the town, officials on both sides said. Lantratova, the Russian human rights commissioner, said Monday that she had expected more people to evacuate from Oleshky, saying “quite a few empty buses” left the area. Many people chose to stay because they couldn’t leave elderly or sick loved ones, she said, or simply refused to leave their homes no matter what. She said for those remaining, humanitarian aid deliveries would take place at least monthly, with the “coordination and mediation” of Melania Trump. Ukraine’s armed forces accused Russia on Monday of using the truce to rotate its units and fortify positions in the area. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Kyiv also could have used the ceasefire to regroup, calling it a “completely common practice in such situations.”
