articles.title: Haley Stevens defends endorsement switch to Republican Mike Rogers over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed
articles.summary: But she refuses to be drawn on her rationale for switching candidates in the closely-fought US Senate race.
articles.body:
A prominent Michigan Democrat who switched her endorsement to the Republican candidate in the final days of the vital Senate race has defended her decision, saying simply: "I changed my mind".

Haley Stevens, who unsuccessfully ran to become the Democratic nominee, withdrew support for the Democratic candidate who beat her in the primary contest, Abdul El-Sayed.

Ahead of the US midterm elections on Tuesday, Stevens gave her last-minute backing to Republican Mike Rogers, sparking widespread condemnation from her Democratic colleagues.

Stevens and El-Sayed have clashed on a range of issues, including US support for Israel. Michigan is considered critical for Democrats' hopes of winning control of Congress in the midterms.

Hours after the announcement, appearing on CNN, she said: "I woke up this morning clear-eyed, fresh and focused on what was in my heart, and that's that."

The seat is currently in Democratic hands. Analysts say the party needs to retain it, and win a handful of others from the Republicans, if it is to gain control of the US Senate and try to challenge US President Donald Trump in his final two years.

Stevens had previously offered her endorsement to El-Sayed after conceding defeat to him during a closely-fought primary contest in August.

As recently as Saturday night, she was said by CNN to be sticking with the fellow Democrat, and was denying any suggestion she would switch sides.

In her interview with the network the following day, Stevens did not provide her specific rationale, saying: "I changed my mind. (El-Sayed) said, 'Hey, I don't need your endorsement.' That's fine. Why the anger? Why the frustration?"

Stevens insisted that "nothing with me changed". She added that she was now "rock solid" in her choice to back Rogers, although insisted: "I still love my party a whole lot."

Fellow Democrats who condemned the Stevens endorsement were also critical of her interview performance. It was described as "painful" by Debbie Dingell, who, like Stevens, currently represents Michigan in the House of Representatives.

Democrat endorses Republican candidate in key Michigan Senate race as party spat erupts

A public feud between Stevens, a centrist Democrat, and El-Sayed, who represents the party's left wing, has boiled over in recent days.

Stevens gave her endorsement to Rogers just two days before the election - making a surprise appearance alongside the Republican on Sunday.

"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted to X shortly afterwards. "Who we are as Michiganders is not hate," and then went on to say: "That's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers," Stevens said.

The move stunned many of her fellow party members, who condemned her decision to switch her support just two days before the election.

Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the US Senate, called it "despicable betrayal", and many of the Stevens staff reportedly resigned immediately after her announcement.

Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel wrote on X that Stevens is "not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future".

Republicans, meanwhile, applauded the move. Rogers himself said the move showed "courage", and Trump agreed that Stevens had been "very brave".

Stevens's schedule for Sunday initially involved her appearing at an event alongside El-Sayed, but she was reportedly asked by him not to come earlier in the weekend.

As Stevens instead made her appearance alongside Rogers, she said: "This is a very close election, we all know that, but Abdul made clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn't need me there, that he didn't want me there."

When asked about Stevens' endorsement, El-Sayed told reporters he was focused on the problems that were facing people in the state.

"At the end of the day, I don't think about Haley Stevens," he said on Sunday. "None of this matters."

Throughout the Michigan race, El-Sayed's strong criticism of Israel has been a source of tension within his party.

A recent flashpoint involved an advert that came from an outside liberal group. The advert linked rising prices in the US with American support for Israel. Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn it. El-Sayed said he did not agree with the advert's contents and said he had nothing to do with its contents, which was welcomed by Stevens.

The Michigan contest more broadly is one of the most closely-watched and bitter contests of the midterms.

El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim person ever elected to the US Senate, has faced a variety of attacks from Rogers and Trump.

The president has invoked 9/11 and called him a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.

articles.title: A California accountant told investors their money would fund backyard homes, but no homes were built and more than $8.2 million vanished in risky trading; he has now been sentenced to 63 months in prison
articles.summary: A 30-year-old California accountant who persuaded people to invest millions of dollars in plans to build small homes on residential properties has been
articles.body: A 30-year-old California accountant who persuaded people to invest millions of dollars in plans to build small homes on residential properties has been sentenced to 63 months in federal prison after admitting that he used their money for risky financial trading instead.Ethan Joseph Sanchez, from San Diego, took more than $8.2 million from investors by promising to use their funds for real estate projects, including the construction of accessory dwelling units (ADUs). However, no such homes were built, and the money was lost through risky day trading, according to the US Department of Justice.US District Judge Robert S Huie sentenced Sanchez on Friday and ordered him to forfeit more than $8.2 million. He was also directed to pay restitution to the victims, although the Justice Department's announcement did not specify a separate restitution amount.Sanchez was a Certified Public Accountant (CPA) when he carried out the scheme. According to his plea agreement, he repeatedly gave investors false information about how their money would be used. He convinced them to lend money to him and his company, BSC Equity Ventures, LLC, by presenting the investments as opportunities to finance real estate transactions.The investors were told that their money would help build additional homes on specified properties and that they would receive their original investment back along with interest. Instead, Sanchez put the funds into risky day trades. The Justice Department said he rarely returned money to investors and did not finance any of the promised real estate projects.How investment scheme workedThe investment opportunity presented by Sanchez involved accessory dwelling units, commonly known as ADUs. These are additional residential units built on properties that already have a main home. They are sometimes described as backyard homes.According to prosecutors, Sanchez used plans involving such units to convince people that their money would support property development. His promises were not limited to construction. He also claimed that investors' funds would be used for other real estate transactions.The arrangement involved people lending money directly to Sanchez or his business. In return, he promised to repay the amount they had provided, along with interest, within the agreed period.However, the money did not go towards the purposes he described. Sanchez admitted that he neither funded real estate transactions nor constructed any of the ADUs he had promised investors.Instead, he used the money for day trading, a form of financial trading involving buying and selling investments over short periods. The trades were risky, and Sanchez lost the investors' money. The scheme ultimately resulted in losses exceeding $8.2 million.Victims describe the impact of lossSeveral victims addressed the court during Sanchez's sentencing hearing, describing how the fraud had affected their lives.One victim spoke about the suffering caused by Sanchez and expressed relief that investigators had uncovered the scheme. “He was caught by the FBI, thank God,” the victim told the court, as quoted by the Justice Department.Judge Huie also spoke about the damage caused by Sanchez's actions. He described the scheme as “aggravated and reprehensible” and pointed out that Sanchez had used existing investors to attract more people into the arrangement.In some cases, those investors persuaded their own family members to participate.The judge described the harm suffered by the victims as “almost unimaginable”. He said the consequences extended beyond the money they had lost, affecting people who had worked to earn and save those funds.The court heard that the financial losses had caused serious personal suffering. Judge Huie described the damage as moving and heartbreaking, making clear that the consequences of the fraud were not limited to the amount stolen.Court orders repayment and prison sentenceFollowing the sentencing hearing, US Attorney Adam Gordon said Sanchez had taken advantage of people who trusted him with their savings.“Ethan Sanchez exploited the trust of hardworking people and stole their savings through lies and fabricated investments. This sentence reflects the profound harm he caused," Gordon said.The federal court imposed a prison term of 63 months, equivalent to five years and three months. Sanchez was also ordered to forfeit more than $8.2 million and pay restitution to those affected.The case involved wire fraud and money laundering charges. articles.title: Iliana Yotova wins runoff to become Bulgaria’s first elected female president
articles.summary: Acting President Iliana Yotova won the runoff election to become Bulgaria’s first elected female head of state and said she will work for national consensus by bridging political rifts.
articles.body: Acting President Iliana Yotova won the runoff election to become Bulgaria’s first elected female head of state and said she will work for national consensus by bridging political rifts. With all the votes counted on Monday, the Central Election Commission said Yotova secured 57.6%, while the candidate of the liberal, pro-Western opposition, Andrey Gyurov, received 39.5%. Gyurov conceded defeat, saying that “this is how the Bulgarian citizens have voted,” and added that the results had to be accepted as they stood. “I voted for national consensus through dialogue, for institutions that work for citizens, for a strong state with its own foreign policy in a strong Europe,” Yotova said after the vote. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Yotova and looked forward to continuing cooperation with her on security and defense, competitiveness, and energy independence. “For a strong Bulgaria in a strong Europe,” von der Leyen wrote in a post on X. The vote was the first major test for Prime Minister Rumen Radev’s Moscow-friendly Progressive Bulgaria party, which endorsed Yotova. In April’s parliamentary vote, the party won 131 of the 240 seats in Parliament, securing an outright majority. Observers note that a victory for Yotova will keep the presidency in the hands of the governing majority. Such a concentration of power could prevent the effective maintenance of checks and balances on policy decisions by institutions, they say. Both Yotova and Radev have called for a diplomatic solution to end the war in Ukraine but remain evasive about possible Russian involvement in drone attacks in the Black Sea region. Yotova has opposed further Bulgarian military assistance to Ukraine, repeatedly arguing that the conflict has no military solution and calling for a “coalition for peace” focused on diplomacy. Yotova, 62, took over the presidency in January, when Radev stepped down to run for parliament, and was seeking her own elected mandate. She’s expected to continue Radev’s policy of keeping Bulgaria on its European path while also supporting better relations with Russia and the lifting of sanctions. Yotova’s professional career began as a TV journalist in the 1990s. Later, she entered politics and was elected to the national Parliament, and later the European Parliament, on the ticket of the Socialist party. In 2016 and 2021 she was elected as Radev’s vice president. Yotova shared her victory with Kiril Valchev, whom she had picked as vice president. Valchev, a 53-year-old lawyer and journalist, had been at the helm of the official Bulgarian News Agency since 2021. The Balkan country joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007. While there is a broad consensus among the parties in parliament on the country’s pro-Western path, widespread pro-Russia sentiment based on traditional historical and cultural ties with Russia has divided society, particularly since the start of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Bulgaria’s presidency is primarily ceremonial. Although the head of state has no executive powers and all major policies must be approved by parliament, direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces and can veto legislation, signs international treaties and appoints ambassadors. Presidents in Bulgaria are elected for a five-year term and can serve no more than two terms. Yotova is expected to be inaugurated on Jan. 22.

articles.summary: Conservative commentator Ann Coulter has publicly expressed support for Indian-American Republican candidate Saritha Komatireddy in the New York attorney
articles.body: Conservative commentator Ann Coulter has publicly expressed support for Indian-American Republican candidate Saritha Komatireddy in the New York attorney general race, saying she wants to vote for her while questioning why she is polling at just 5%."Finally an Indian I'd vote for and SHE'S AT 5%??? What kind of country is this?" Coulter wrote in a post on X (formerly Twitter) on November 2, reacting to the betting odds for the New York attorney general election.Komatireddy is the Republican and Conservative Party candidate challenging incumbent Democratic Attorney General Letitia James in the November 3 midterm elections.Coulter's remarks have attracted attention because of her previous comments about another Indian-American Republican politician, Vivek Ramaswamy. During an appearance on Ramaswamy's podcast in May 2024, Coulter told him she would not have voted for him in the presidential election because he was Indian."I still would not have voted for you, because you're an Indian," she told Ramaswamy.The former Republican presidential candidate later acknowledged her remarks in a post on X, saying Coulter had told him directly that she could not vote for him because he was Indian, even though she agreed with him on several issues.Coulter's latest comment about Komatireddy has therefore drawn attention as she publicly expressed a willingness to vote for an Indian-American candidate.Who is Saritha Komatireddy?Saritha Komatireddy is a former federal prosecutor, a lecturer at Columbia Law School and a former chief of staff of the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).She served as an assistant US attorney in the Eastern District of New York, where she held several leadership positions involving national security, cybercrime, narcotics and money laundering cases. She also served as the DEA's chief of staff from 2023 to 2024.A Harvard College and Harvard Law School graduate, Komatireddy was also nominated by President Donald Trump in 2020 to serve as a federal judge in the Eastern District of New York. Her nomination was not confirmed by the Senate.She is now a partner at the law firm Holtzman Vogel and teaches at Columbia Law School.Komatireddy is challenging Letitia James, who has served as New York attorney general since 2019.What is Komatireddy promising?Public safety is a central theme of Komatireddy's campaign. She has called for tougher action against repeat offenders, changes to New York's bail policies and stronger prosecution of crime.She has also made government fraud and corruption investigations part of her campaign platform.In interviews, Komatireddy has criticised James's approach to public safety and argued that the attorney general's office should do more to tackle crime and fraud.Why did Coulter mention the 5% figure?Coulter's post referred to betting-market odds for the New York attorney general contest. A market-tracking report on November 2 put Komatireddy at around 5%, compared with approximately 95% for James.The figures represent market-implied probabilities, not the percentage of voters supporting either candidate. articles.title: Karl Bushby completes 28-year, 31,000-mile walk around world and returns to mother’s house
articles.summary: HULL, England (AP) — Karl Bushby embraced his weeping mother in his arms Monday as he returned to his northern England home to complete a 28-year odyssey to...
articles.body:
HULL, England (AP) — Karl Bushby embraced his weeping mother in his arms Monday as he returned to his northern England home to complete a 28-year odyssey to walk around the world .

"Where have you been?" his mother, Angela, asked as he arrived outside the home he left in 1998 that was now decked with a banner saying "Welcome Home Son."

Bushby set out from Punta Arenas, Chile, on Nov. 1, 1998, and walked 31,000 miles (50,000 kilometers) across four continents and 30 countries to get home. He navigated shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel to avoid taking a boat or plane — or any transport — to propel him forward.

He vowed not to return until he could complete the journey on foot. It was an eye-opening adventure full of danger and drudgery that was interrupted for years at a time by the unexpected: the 2008 financial crash that sapped funding from sponsors, the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic and mountains of bureaucratic red tape to get across international borders.

On the final day of the journey, Bushby pushed his cart toward a hero's welcome at City Hall before setting off for the last stretch to see his mother.

"Sorry to keep you waiting," he joked to the crowd of hundreds who cheered his arrival. "Is that it, is it done?"

The ex-paratrooper said he looked like he was 10 years old when he left his mother's rowhouse at the age of 29. He returned as a 57-year-old — softer, grayer and weathered, but far more worldly.

"They say it takes a village but literally it took a world to get me here," Bushby said. "The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation states to get me back here today. I didn't do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth."

The idea started with a birthday card from his dad

Bushby had a thirst for adventure, but his mission only came into focus when his father, Keith, sent him a birthday card in the mid-90s. His dad, an army veteran himself, mentioned an argument two special forces troops had about the possibility of walking from London to New York over the Bering land bridge, believed by some scientists to have been used by early humans to migrate from Asia to the Americas at a time of lower sea levels.

Perilous jungles, scorching deserts and frozen tundra slowed him down, but bureaucratic holdups brought his adventure to a halt for long periods.

Bushby originally calculated the distance could be covered in about five years, but he knew that was unrealistic.

"You just dump a whole bucket full of reality on that," he said. "We suspected that it was 12 years plus. And the plus was a big plus. But never in our wildest dreams would we ever have imagined 28 years."

Danger on land and sea followed by border problems

He dodged war in the dangerous Darién Gap, the roadless and rugged jungle, rainforest and mountains between South and Central America in 2001, and was then jailed for 18 days after crossing a restricted border zone in Panama.

After being airlifted to safety during the 56-mile (90-kilometer) Bering Strait crossing in 2006 with American adventurer Dimitry Kieffer, they started again and faced a standoff with a polar bear, survived near-death plunges into freezing waters and almost lost all their supplies when their sleds plunged in the sea. After managing the rare crossing, the pair were jailed and faced deportation for entering Russia illegally.

It took Bushby almost 10 years to make his way through Russia in fits and starts because of visa struggles and weather that only allowed travel a few months a year. When Russia denied him a visa in 2012, Bushby walked in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork.

Family firsts and a long-awaited reunion

Bushby has met several times over the decades with family members who have met up with him on his journey. He was greeted on the beach in Dover by his father and brothers after crossing the channel last month.

He reunited with Adam, his 36-year-old son from an early marriage whom he had rarely seen, and he met his 12-year-old granddaughter for the first time.

Bushby hadn't seen his mother in a decade, setting the stage for an emotional and somewhat awkward reunion captured amid a throng of cameras and a documentary film crew.

"Behave yourself, mother," he joked, as his mother wept and he held her and rubbed her back. "Get yourself together."

In the final days of his trip, Bushby spoke of his anxiety over the trip ending, living in his mom's basement and not knowing what he would do.

"It's like stepping across the event horizon into a black hole," he told The Associated Press. "I have no idea what's about to happen in my life."

articles.title: Historic flooding forces evacuations in Southwest as storm shifts east for Election Day
articles.summary: Rivers are bursting their banks after multiple months’ worth of rain. Now, voter turnout could be impacted by the storm.
articles.body: A storm causing historic flooding, evacuations and rescues in the Southwest is now pushing into the central United States, where it will bring soggy weather on Election Day on Tuesday. The conditions will be much less serious on Election Day but could still affect turnout in key races across the nation’s midsection. Active weather tends to suppress voter turnout while sunshine has the opposite effect, multiple studies have found. Rain is finally easing up in the Southwest after the storm dropped multiple months’ worth of it, causing waterways to burst their banks and forcing evacuations in a least a dozen counties across parts of Arizona, Colorado and New Mexico. Crews in Arizona are still searching for a missing man who fell into fast-moving floodwater in Flagstaff and have conducted rooftop rescues around Sedona. Over 10 rivers, creeks and washes in Arizona and southwest Colorado have now surged past major flood stage — the highest level — and a few have set new record crests. Flooding of some swollen waterways could last through at least Tuesday. Record flooding is unfolding along the Little Colorado River near Winslow, Arizona, and the Gila River near Solomon, Arizona. The Gila River is more than 2 feet higher than the level capable of flooding several homes and businesses on the north sides of Solomon, Safford and Thatcher, Arizona, according to the National Weather Service. In Colorado, evacuations have been ordered along the San Juan River in Pagosa Springs, which has surged past major flood stage for the second time in about 10 days. Sunday evening’s crest there was nearly 2 feet higher than the destructive flooding on October 23. Storm pushes east for Election Day The storm is now pushing into the Plains and Midwest with gusty winds and soaking rain. Severe thunderstorms are possible Monday afternoon into the night across the central and southern Plains, including in Dallas-Fort Worth, Oklahoma City and Wichita, Kansas. Damaging winds are the primary threat, but a few tornadoes are also possible. The storm will lose some of its strength on Election Day, but rain will impact voters from the Great Plains and Upper Midwest south through the Mississippi Valley to the western Gulf Coast. Key races in Iowa, Kansas, eastern Texas and northern Michigan will deal with wet conditions. Isolated severe storms are possible from eastern Texas to the lower and middle Mississippi Valley. The threat of flooding rain is low, but voters traveling to the polls could encounter ponding on roads. Dry weather will sandwich the storm along much of the East Coast and in the West. Some showers in Florida, northern New England and Northern California are the only exceptions. Across much of the country, there will be little need to bundle up to go vote. High temperatures in most of the nation’s eastern half are forecast to be 5 to 20 degrees Fahrenheit above average. Some portions of the Southwest and Plains will lean a bit cooler than average. articles.title: How US oil firms profit $130bn from Iran war as household bills surge
articles.summary: As energy from the Gulf and Russia take a hit, American oil and gas firms are the big gainers.
articles.body:
United States oil companies have earned more than $130bn in profits during the war on Iran, even as consumers pay much higher prices for key commodities, amid fears that US President Donald Trump may renew fighting after midterm elections .

The estimate, released by The New York Times, is a conservative evaluation based on the performance of 51 large US oil and gas companies in the six months from April through September. By contrast, in the same period in 2025 – when the prices of oil were lower prior to the launch of the US-Israel war on Iran – they collectively earned less than $47bn.

But the gains come as burgeoning living costs are crushing consumers. Americans have spent an extra $150bn on petrol and diesel since the war on Iran began on February 28, according to an analysis by Brown University ’s Climate Solutions Lab, which amounts to more than $1,150 per household.

The disparity has fuelled a political debate over who gains and who pays the price for the war. Responding to Trump, Democratic Representative Jim McGovern wrote on X: “We’re not making a ‘freaking fortune,’ we’re PAYING a ‘freaking fortune’.”

US Big Oil in position to profit where others lose

Naser al-Tamimi, a fellow at the Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI) in Milan, Italy, said US energy companies have benefitted from the war in different ways. “Crude producers gain from higher oil prices, while refiners capture exceptional margins as diesel and other fuel supplies tighten,” he said.

Additionally, “damage to Middle Eastern and Russian refineries, disrupted Strait of Hormuz shipments , and sanctions-related trade frictions have intensified shortages”, while “relatively secure US facilities and access to discounted crude strengthen these gains”.

ExxonMobil and Chevron, the biggest US oil companies, on Friday reported profits of between $10bn and $15bn. While the gains are considerable, The New York Times found they generally remained below 2022 levels, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused oil prices to soar to roughly $100 a barrel and raised natural gas prices, compared with the current average of $90 from April through September.

American refining companies also reaped greater profits as global fuel supplies tightened and inventories depleted due to heavy damage to infrastructure in the Middle East and Russia. Valero Energy’s third-quarter profit increased more than sixfold, reaching $6.83bn. Phillips 66 announced its highest quarterly profit on record, with net income jumping to $5.62bn from $133m a year earlier.

Geoffrey Miller, geopolitical analyst and editor of the Gulf States Insights newsletter, said the US-Israel war with Iran “created the largest supply-side shock to global oil and refined products markets in years”.

Miller added that the war “created a risk premium that US-based operators are structurally well placed to monetise”. By contrast, Gulf producers were “hit hard by both higher costs and risks, along with physical damage, which makes their ability to benefit from the higher prices much more difficult”.

Tehran retaliated against the US-Israeli attack by launching missiles and drones at the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC). The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), a US-registered independent conflict monitor, found Iran and Iran-backed groups in the region have carried out at least 172 attacks on nonmilitary infrastructure across the six GCC member states. Despite claims by Iranian officials that they were targeting US military facilities, they also hit energy infrastructure.

Iran also effectively blocked passage of most vessels through the Strait of Hormuz. In retaliation, the US imposed a naval blockade on Iranian oil and gas – the tit-for-tat steps raising the risks of transporting energy out of the crucial passageway.

Analysts warned of continued volatility until a durable political settlement between the US and Iran is reached. Oil prices dropped briefly in the summer after a memorandum of understanding was signed in June, but prices quickly soared again when talks broke down.

A more recent escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has further compounded the crisis: the Bab al-Mandeb strait that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, which Saudi Arabia uses to export oil, is now also a theatre of war.

“In the short term, windfall profits will only strengthen oil company balance sheets and shareholder returns,” Miller said. “However, the big profits come with a major caveat. That’s because over the longer term, high oil prices risk harming economic growth prospects and could even contribute towards the outbreak of a recession, which would in turn be likely to lead to reduced demand for oil” and accelerate the transition to renewable energy.

Florence Schmit, senior energy strategist at Rabobank’s global economics and markets team in London, said it was likely that the prices of key energy products would remain high given the uncertainty about the duration of the war in Iran.

“Prices in all markets that have an exposure to this global supply shock – which includes the US – will face high prices also next year, and consumers will continue to feel this price pressure unless governments step in,” Schmit told Al Jazeera.

The US-led war on Iran has raised costs for oil, transport fuels, gas, electricity and food. According to the World Bank Group’s latest Commodity Markets Outlook, commodity prices are set to rise 23 percent this year, as disrupted grain shipments and the El Nino weather phenomenon also threaten harvests and food affordability.

The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization said on October 2 that world food commodity prices rose a further 1.5 percent in September, after reaching their highest level since late 2022 in August, amid adverse weather and trade disruptions in the Black Sea and Strait of Hormuz.

Trump has sought to blame high global fuel prices on Ukraine and pressured Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian refineries, even as Moscow continued to wage attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The US president has argued that a deal with Russia reversing years of sanctions would help lower diesel prices.

In the Gulf, analysts said higher oil prices will benefit exporters that can maintain shipments, but prolonged insecurity will continue to threaten supply reliability and investment.

“Gulf producers face years of reconstruction and pressure to diversify export routes,” ISPI’s al-Tamimi said. “A diplomatic settlement could ease prices, whereas renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran risk triggering another regional war, further disrupting Hormuz and prolonging shortages.”

articles.title: Rare Salvador Dali lithograph collection to go under the hammer
articles.summary: The artworks are being sold by a private collector who is moving abroad and are expected to fetch as much as £120,000.
articles.body:
A private art collection which includes more than 30 hand-signed Salvador Dali lithographs is to go up for auction.

The images are being prepared for public display in Glasgow before going under the hammer on 24 November, when they are expected to fetch as much as £120,000.

Eric Crombie, from Crombie's Auctioneers, said the owner of the collection had got in touch as he is moving abroad and cannot take the lithographs with him.

He said: "Finding a single authenticated, hand-signed Dali is rare, but uncovering an entire private collection of this scale is a major event for the art world."

Speaking to BBC Radio Scotland's Lunchtime Live , Crombie said they were "delighted" to have the collection.

"It's massive for us as a small auction house", he added.

The lithographs are prints that are signed by the Spanish artist, who was a leading figure in the surrealist movement.

"To kind of put it in perspective there's never been a private collection of this size certainly in recent times to come up for auction," he said.

He said one of the highlights of the collections was the Conquest of the Cosmos - a set of six pieces exploring themes of space, science and the universe - that are still in the original box from 1974.

"Normally they've been broke up throughout the year so to find a complete set in the original box is kind of unheard of really."

He said they were still going through the collection, which also contained works from another Spanish artist.

"There's that much of it... we are still uncovering it because a lot of it was prepared to be stored, so we are just uncovering it now, but we reckon that between the collection is going to be possibly between £80,000 and £120,000."

Crombie added that the auction catalogue would be available to view online from Thursday, while the artworks would be available to view in person from 21 November until the auction.

The actual sale itself will be available to view in person up until the auction at 18:00 on 24 November.

articles.title: Special court reserves order in appeals challenging bail in Cheranalloor accident case
articles.summary: Special court in Ernakulam reserves order on appeals against bail for 17-year-old in Cheranalloor accident case; SIT probes evidence destruction claim.
articles.body: Kochi: The special court for considering cases involving atrocities against women and children in Ernakulam on Monday reserved its order in the criminal appeals against the bail granted to the 17-year-old juvenile involved in the Cheranalloor accident.The court is likely to pass an order on Thursday. A dramatic situation prevailed in the court as the prosecution and counsel for the victim’s family exchanged allegations in the court. The judge later decided to conduct further proceedings in camera considering the involvement of a child in conflict with the law.Earlier, Bhadrakeerthy R J, the daughter of the deceased Jayabalakrishnan, had told the media that the family lacked confidence in the prosecution. The prosecutor on Monday raised the issue before the court, accusing the victim’s family of interfering with the independent investigation through contradictory statements to the media.The court observed that it was a serious matter and sought clarification on whether such interference had indeed occurred. Adv M G Sreejith, counsel for the family, accused the prosecution of non-cooperation while denying the allegation. The court noted that the special public prosecutor had been serving in the court for seven years and observed that any grievances should have been raised before the court. Sreejith later downplayed the matter before the media, saying that the family and the prosecution have the same objective.Meanwhile, the SIT will investigate the complaint filed by Bhadrakeerthy accusing the father of the juvenile, a sessions judge, of destruction of evidence in the case.
